candidates.speaker: Daniel Dennett
candidates.proposition: The freedom relevant to moral responsibility is compatible with determinism and consists in ordinary responsible agency rather than libertarian metaphysics.
candidates.attributionBasis: The microphone handoff identifies Dennett, and the uninterrupted turn continues until Harris explicitly begins responding.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This establishes the compatibilist answer to the motion by separating responsibility-grounding freedom from indeterministic or agent-causal freedom.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Harris's earlier portrayal of Dennett's compatibilism as quasi-theological and as failing to acknowledge that free will is unreal.

candidates.contextSummary: Dennett stresses extensive agreement about rejecting libertarianism, then locates valuable freedom in competent, uncoerced agency that supports contracts, responsibility, and justified punishment.

candidates.speaker: Daniel Dennett
candidates.proposition: Compatibilism legitimately preserves a naturalistic meaning of free will by refining inherited concepts instead of treating their magical interpretations as definitive.
candidates.attributionBasis: Harris invites Dennett to define compatibilism, after which Dennett speaks continuously until Harris poses his objection.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This supplies the conceptual methodology behind Dennett's position and explains why rejecting a magical definition need not require abandoning free-will language.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Harris's claim that compatibilism resembles theology and does not identify a serious form of free will.

candidates.contextSummary: Dennett treats disputes over whether consciousness or free will exists as partly diplomatic choices between eliminating a misleading concept and retaining a purified naturalistic version.

candidates.speaker: Sam Harris
candidates.proposition: Compatibilism risks changing the subject because purifying a concept can discard features that are indispensable to what people mean by free will.
candidates.attributionBasis: The turn begins as a direct objection to Dennett's preceding account and ends when Dennett immediately answers it.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This frames Harris's principal conceptual objection: the compatibilist phenomenon may be real while failing to answer the original free-will concern.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Dennett's claim that free will can truthfully be said to exist once its magical and traditional baggage is removed.

candidates.contextSummary: Harris distinguishes scientifically explaining a real phenomenon from redefining it so extensively that the supposedly preserved concept no longer addresses its core concern.

candidates.speaker: Daniel Dennett
candidates.proposition: Free will is the reasons-responsive competence to control an agent's many practical degrees of freedom, and this capacity—not indeterminism—grounds responsibility.
candidates.attributionBasis: Dennett directly takes up Harris's objection and retains the microphone throughout the extended engineering and responsible-agent account.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This is the central positive compatibilist model, connecting freedom, rational control, self-control, absence of usurpation, and moral responsibility.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Harris's objection that compatibilism merely changes the subject by eliminating the concept's essential incompatibilist feature.

candidates.contextSummary: Dennett rejects a sharp line between clarification and subject change, then models freedom through controllable capacities, responsiveness to reasons, and the distinction between competent agents and constrained or controlled ones.

candidates.speaker: Sam Harris
candidates.proposition: The enduring free-will problem concerns first-person authorship and the ability to do otherwise, neither of which is supported by determinism or indeterminism.
candidates.attributionBasis: Harris begins after acknowledging Dennett's account and speaks continuously through a sustained first-person analysis of agency.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This identifies the experiential and metaphysical target Harris believes compatibilism misses and gives his direct argument against conscious authorship.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Dennett's account of free will as reasons-responsive control that can be fully distinguished within either a deterministic or indeterministic world.

candidates.contextSummary: Harris separates first-person experience from third-person functional description, denies that an exact replay permits another choice, and argues that thoughts simply arise from unconscious processes.

candidates.speaker: Sam Harris
candidates.proposition: Compatibilism preserves real capacities but calls them free will in the way one might preserve Sicily while abandoning the fictional features that made Atlantis the subject of interest.
candidates.attributionBasis: The same Harris turn explicitly introduces an analogy from his prior response and develops it until Dennett answers.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The analogy sharpens the subject-changing objection by conceding compatibilist facts while denying that they answer the motivating first-person claim.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Dennett's proposal to retain free-will language for naturalistic capacities after removing libertarian and magical commitments.

candidates.contextSummary: Harris compares rejecting libertarian freedom while retaining compatibilist agency to rejecting mythical Atlantis while redirecting attention to a real island sharing peripheral features.

candidates.speaker: Daniel Dennett
candidates.proposition: A nonmagical form of free will preserves the responsibility distinctions people need, while the experience of deciding requires treating some possibilities as open without requiring absolute metaphysical openness.
candidates.attributionBasis: Dennett explicitly reconstructs Harris's position and then delivers a continuous response about naturalistic responsibility and deliberation.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This directly answers both the subject-changing charge and the experiential challenge by arguing that practical agency supplies the freedom worth preserving.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Harris's Atlantis analogy and his claim that people's felt ability to do otherwise is the indispensable feature compatibilism abandons.

candidates.contextSummary: Dennett concedes that magical freedom does not exist but argues that naturalistic agency retains daily responsibility practices and that deliberation necessarily represents alternatives as unsettled.

candidates.speaker: Daniel Dennett
candidates.proposition: An agent can meaningfully have been able to do otherwise when a small variation would produce another choice, even if the decision process itself is deterministic.
candidates.attributionBasis: Dennett continues the same uninterrupted turn, using a deterministic chess program to clarify counterfactual ability and design competence.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This provides a concrete compatibilist analysis of alternative possibilities and separates unlucky outcomes from defects in an agent's decision-making design.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Harris's exact-replay standard under which an agent could not have done otherwise unless the identical prior state produced a different result.

candidates.contextSummary: A deterministic chess program can lose after one pseudo-random result while remaining well designed; nearby variations support an ordinary counterfactual sense in which it could have chosen differently.

candidates.speaker: Sam Harris
candidates.proposition: Dependence of major life choices on minute neural differences is deeply subversive of ordinary personhood because it makes the universe, rather than a conscious self, control the outcome.
candidates.attributionBasis: Harris takes the microphone with an explicit concession followed by a sustained objection, ending when Dennett begins his answer.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This explains why accepting compatibilist counterfactuals does not resolve Harris's concern: causal sensitivity itself revives the loss-of-authorship problem.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Dennett's deterministic chess example and claim that tiny variations can justify saying a well-designed agent could have acted otherwise.

candidates.contextSummary: Harris accepts the functional analysis but argues that tiny neurophysiological contingencies controlling transformative choices conflict with how people experience themselves as authors of their lives.

candidates.speaker: Daniel Dennett
candidates.proposition: Neither absolute indeterminacy nor sensitivity to tiny changes defeats freedom: close decisions may flip under small variations, while reason-dominated decisions require much larger changes.
candidates.attributionBasis: Dennett explicitly answers Harris's immediately preceding objection and continues beyond the owned core through the available boundary context.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This distinguishes genuine toss-ups from decisions settled by reasons and argues that determination can express, rather than negate, responsible agency.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Harris's claim that minute physical contingencies behind consequential choices restore marionette-like control by the universe and undermine personhood.

candidates.contextSummary: Dennett calls absolute undetermination irrelevant, distinguishes finely balanced choices from strongly reason-governed ones, and begins using a determined yet responsibility-affirming decision as a counterexample.
